passages.t: After the curse: return, and a new heart
passages.happening:
Moses looks past the curses of chapter 28 to what comes after them. He speaks of a day when all these things have happened, and Israel is scattered among the nations and calls them to mind (verse 1).

When ‘you and your children return to the LORD your God and obey His voice with all your heart and all your soul’, then God ‘will restore you from captivity and have compassion on you and gather you from all the nations to which the LORD your God has scattered you’ (verses 2-3). “Even if you have been banished to the farthest horizon, He will gather you and return you from there” (verse 4).

Then the promise at the center of the passage. “The LORD your God will circumcise your hearts and the hearts of your descendants, and you will love Him with all your heart and with all your soul, so that you may live” (verse 6).

Israel will obey again, and God will again delight in his people, ‘as He delighted in that of your fathers’ (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
The opening words are remarkable. Moses does not say ‘if’ these things come upon Israel. He says ‘when’. He speaks as one who knows that the curse will fall, and he speaks to the people who will be living under it.

So this chapter is addressed to failure. It is spoken to a people who have done the worst and lost everything, and it tells them that the story is not over.

The passage is built on one Hebrew verb, shuv, which means to turn or to return. It comes again and again, and it is used both of Israel and of God. Israel returns to the LORD, which is repentance. And the LORD returns Israel to the land, which is restoration. The prophets later made this their chief word for repentance.

Look at how far the promise reaches. It reaches to ‘the farthest horizon’. There is no distance at which God cannot find his people.

Then verse 6. In chapter 10 Moses commanded, ‘Circumcise your hearts’. The people could not do it. Chapter 29 admitted that they did not yet have a heart to understand. Now God says that he will do it himself. Circumcision was the outward sign of the covenant. A circumcised heart is the inward thing the sign pointed to: a heart cut free from stubbornness and given to God. And the result is the Shema fulfilled: ‘you will love Him with all your heart and with all your soul’.

This is the deepest hope in Deuteronomy. The book that commands love ends by promising that God will make that love possible.

Jews in exile did read these words as a promise that their scattering was not God's last word. Whether the chapter was spoken by Moses long beforehand, or took its final shape during the exile, as many critical scholars think, readers on both sides agree on that.
passages.later:
Nehemiah, in exile, prayed this passage back to God almost word for word: ‘even if your exiles have been banished to the farthest horizon, I will gather them from there’ (Nehemiah 1:9).

Jeremiah wrote the same promise to the exiles in Babylon: “I will be found by you, declares the LORD, and I will restore you from captivity” (Jeremiah 29:14).

Paul says that what verse 6 promises is the work of God's Spirit: ‘circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the written code’ (Romans 2:29).

Jesus told a story of a son in a far country who ‘came to his senses’ and turned for home. “But while he was still in the distance, his father saw him and was filled with compassion” (Luke 15:20).
passages.asks: This passage is written for people who have already failed. Ask whether there is a failure in your life that you think has put you beyond the reach of a new beginning. Then read verse 4 again. And ask God to do in your heart what verse 6 says he does, since it is something you cannot do for yourself.

passages.happening:
Moses turns to speak about the command itself. “For this commandment I give you today is not too difficult for you or beyond your reach” (verse 11).

It is not in heaven, so that someone would have to go up and fetch it (verse 12). It is not across the sea, so that someone would have to make the crossing and bring it back (verse 13).

“But the word is very near you; it is in your mouth and in your heart, so that you may obey it” (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
In the world around Israel people sought the will of the gods through diviners and omens, as chapter 18 describes.

Moses says that Israel is in a different position. God has spoken. No one has to climb to heaven or sail to the end of the world to find out what he wants. He has put it into plain words and given it to ordinary people.

‘In your mouth’ means that Israel can say it. The words have been taught and recited. ‘In your heart’ means that they are meant to be taken inside, as chapter 6 commanded.

The Hebrew word for ‘near’ is the point. Moses is not saying that obedience is easy. He is saying that God's will is not hidden. It is close, clear and already given. No one can plead that he did not know.

Jewish tradition has long read these verses as a joyful assurance. The Torah is a gift that can be lived, given to people on earth and not kept in heaven.
passages.later:
Chapter 4 said the same of God himself: no other nation has ‘a god as near to them as the LORD our God is to us whenever we call on Him’ (Deuteronomy 4:7).

Paul quotes this passage in Romans 10. The righteousness that comes by faith, he says, does not ask, ‘Who will ascend into heaven?’ as though Christ had to be brought down, or who will go down to the depths, as though Christ had to be brought up from the dead. “But what does it say? ‘The word is near you; it is in your mouth and in your heart,’ that is, the word of faith we are proclaiming” (Romans 10:8). In Moses' setting the word is God's law, given and near. Paul reads the passage in the light of Christ: the word now near is the message about him.
passages.hard:
Chapter 29 says that Israel had not been given a heart to understand. How can Moses now say that the command is not too difficult? And is Paul right to use these verses of Christ?

On the first question, readers answer in a few ways. Some stress that verse 11 is about how clear and how available the command is, and not about human ability. God has not hidden his will, so no one can plead ignorance. Others note that the law already made provision for failure, through sacrifice and forgiveness, so that faithful life under the covenant never meant being without sin. Many Christian readers, following Paul, see the answer in the chapter itself: the command can truly be kept when God circumcises the heart (verse 6). Jewish tradition reads the passage as an assurance that the Torah is a gift that can be lived. These readings overlap more than they conflict.

On the second, Paul does not claim that Moses was speaking of Christ in so many words. He takes Moses' point, that God's word has come near and need not be fetched from far away, and says that this has come true in the fullest way: Christ has come down, Christ has been raised, and the message about him is as near as a person's own mouth and heart. Readers differ on whether Paul sets the law and faith against each other here, or reads Deuteronomy as the law itself pointing beyond the law. The note on Romans 10 sets out the readings, and these notes do not choose.

Jewish readers do not read the passage as Paul does. For them the word that is near is the Torah, and the disagreement is a real one.
passages.asks: God's will for you is mostly not hidden. Ask what you are waiting to have explained, or proved, or brought nearer, before you do what you already know. And ask whether his word is in your mouth and in your heart, or only on a shelf.

passages.happening:
Moses comes to the end of his preaching. “See, I have set before you today life and goodness, as well as death and disaster” (verse 15).

To love God, to walk in his ways and to keep his commands is the way of life in the land (verse 16). “But if your heart turns away and you do not listen, but are drawn away to bow down to other gods and worship them, I declare to you today that you will surely perish” (verses 17-18).

Then he calls his witnesses and makes his appeal. “I call heaven and earth as witnesses against you today that I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing. Therefore choose life, so that you and your descendants may live, and that you may love the LORD your God, obey Him, and hold fast to Him. For He is your life” (verses 19-20).
passages.hearers:
Everything in the book has led to this. Thirty chapters of story, law, warning and promise are gathered into one choice.

Treaties in the ancient world named the gods of both sides as witnesses. Israel could call on no other god. So Moses calls on heaven and earth, the whole created order, which will still be there when everyone in the crowd is dead.

Notice what the choice is. Moses does not say, choose obedience, or choose the law. He says, ‘choose life’. He speaks as a man pleading. He is an old man who is about to die, and he wants this people to live.

And notice what life is. Verse 20 does not define it as long years or good harvests, though those are promised. It says, ‘He is your life’. To love God, to listen to him and to hold fast to him is itself the life that is offered. The word for ‘hold fast’ is the word used in Genesis for a husband holding fast to his wife.

The word ‘choose’ is striking in this book. Elsewhere it is God who chooses: he chooses Israel, the place of worship, and the king. Here, for once, Israel is told to choose. The command does not deny that God chose first. It calls the chosen people to say yes to it.

The last words go back to the beginning of everything: the land sworn ‘to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob’. The choice set before Israel rests on a promise that is older than Israel.

The chapter has now said two things that must be kept together. God will change the heart (verse 6). And Israel must choose (verse 19). The book does not explain how the two fit. It says both, and leaves neither out.
passages.later:
Joshua put the same choice to the next generation at Shechem: ‘choose for yourselves this day whom you will serve’ (Joshua 24:15).

Isaiah calls the same witnesses when he brings God's case against Israel: “Listen, O heavens, and give ear, O earth, for the LORD has spoken” (Isaiah 1:2).

Jesus speaks of himself in the terms of verse 20: “I am the way and the truth and the life” (John 14:6), and “I have come that they may have life, and have it in all its fullness” (John 10:10).
passages.asks: Moses does not leave the choice general. He says ‘today’. Ask what choosing life would mean for you this week, in one actual decision. And notice that life, in verse 20, is a person to hold on to. Ask whether you are looking for life in God himself or only in what he gives.
